items.evidence: After the title and a one-line italic note on the index ("Every count below is conditional on the local index..."), the overview opens "## The bottom line" with "**1. What FRUS answers directly.** FRUS answers this question directly but unevenly...", then "**2. Where FRUS points for the rest.** FRUS is a selection, so two channels lead to the unprinted record, and they are kept apart here...", then "**3. What this request cannot get from FRUS.** (a) A rate...", followed by Scope, Decisions, and only then "## Findings". The three parts are in the required order and precede every finding.

Every figure carries its set: "About three thousand documents (roughly one in a hundred of the 311,000 documents in the 551 first-edition volumes, once front matter, editorial notes and two duplicate second editions are set aside)"; "On a forty-document test, eight of the forty tie the word... about one in five"; "Of the 38 documents in the collection, 37 carry a source line and one, an 1893 despatch, does not"; "23 of the 37"; the footnote counts are "counted over the roughly three thousand documents that use the vocabulary... Carter Library National Security Affairs (53 citations)"; "The index holds 143 dated documents for the 1840s and 158 for the 1850s, and for the 1990s only 177, from one volume: none of those 177 uses the vocabulary, though 130 of them use 'Department of State'"; "the Central Intelligence Agency appears as the source of 117 of the hit documents"; method: "(40 of 40), 35 of 40 held a basic form, 33 of 40 used the word in the sense of the question and 8 of 40 tied it to an American choice". No bare percentage anywhere; "238 linear feet" is the named Conference Files series' extent, not a count.

All 38 cited documents are given as the printed edition with a link, e.g. "*Foreign Relations of the United States, Diplomatic Papers, 1944, China, Volume VI*, Document 269 (https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1944v06/d269)", "*Foreign Relations of the United States, 1969–1976, Volume E–9, Part 2, Documents on the Middle East Region, 1973–1976*, Document 155 (https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1969-76ve09p2/d155)", and the pre-1932 volumes under their printed titles, "*Papers Relating to the Foreign Relations of the United States, 1922, Volume I*, Document 864 (https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1922v01/d864)" and "*Papers Relating to the Foreign Relations of the United States, With the Annual Message of the President Transmitted to Congress December 3, 1912*, Document 1502 (...)". No citation is by a bare id pair or by title alone, including the repeat references in the findings, which are spelled out in full each time; all 38 appear in the collection.

Item 3(a) states the search: "I searched the corruption vocabulary (corrupt, bribe, graft, embezzle, kickback, and 'illicit' or 'questionable' payments) across all 551 first-edition volumes, with a positive control ('Department of State', found in 94,049 documents and in every volume but one Paris Peace Conference volume) and a negative control (an impossible string, found nowhere)." Item 3(c) makes the 1990s zero a measurement: "for the 1990s only 177, from one volume: none of those 177 uses the vocabulary, though 130 of them use 'Department of State', so the silence is the index's limit." Sub-items (b), (d) and (e) name shelves outside FRUS by nature (foreign archives, the subcommittee's and SEC files, CIA files) rather than absences a search could test, and (e) gives its count, "117 of the hit documents".

The overview contains no SQL, no table or column name and no file path; the method is in words ("I searched the index's full text (which reduces words to roots, so 'corrupt' also finds 'corruption' and 'corrupted')"), the memo is named without a path ("The exact figures and the queries behind them are in the memo"), and the only volume/document id strings are the paths inside the history.state.gov links that J3 requires (e.g. "https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1944v06/d269"); no bare id pair such as frus1944v06/d269 appears in the prose.

judge:s5.rankingReason: s6: the sharpest answer (strategic interest usually won; Koreagate the one clear case of an allegation changing an executive calculation), the model limits section (a pre-1860 search with period vocabulary and both controls), the most thoroughly resolved archival pointers with caveats on NARA titles, 30 documents; its one enormous archival paragraph is the only cost. s5: the widest documented span (38 documents, 1893–1986), the only measured share (8 of 40 tie the word to an American choice), a four-kind typology with an honest close, every citation in full with a link, a clean bulleted archival list and a collection with a note on every document; resolves fewer archival identifiers than s6. s2: 19 documents in a clean bullet-quote structure, the novel bribery-as-instrument finding, an exemplary stepwise FCPA search with controls and rich archival identifiers; a narrower period (1944–1980) by its own choice. s1: 29 documents across five ways and good second-channel lot identifiers, but the findings tack the quotations on after the prose in a hard-to-read run (one with doubled quotation marks) and the control figures sit in the method section rather than beside the claim. s7: meets every criterion and is the most clearly written, with the 1875 claims case and precise identifiers, but rests on only eleven documents. s8: 28 documents and strong episodes (Korean aid made conditional, Nicaragua 1978), but the bottom line and parts of the findings cite documents without links or in abbreviated form ("Document 135 of the 1958–1960 Vietnam volume"; "the Atherton briefing (Document 155)"), so a historian cannot follow them, and the text is hard-wrapped. s3: twelve documents only, the bottom line cites by abbreviated references without links ("1944, Volume VI, Document 292") and the findings drop the series title; honest about its thinness but gives the historian the least.

score:s5.notes: All four files are present (memo.md, overview.md, collection.fruscollection, queries.log), with the helper scripts and outputs the log names on disk in the run directory. Independent verification against the read-only copy: coverage 553|321749|1103|8481, non-apparatus 312,169, Ed2 740, family 3058|447, `corrupt` 2175|399, positive control 94049|552, 1990s 177 documents in 1 volume with family 0 and control 130, pointed-at anchors 450/176/138, CIA came-from 117, `pecul*` 3,140 and `peculat` 0 — every figure reproduces. All 22 overview quotations and all 22 collection excerpts are substrings of the named document's body_text; the collection holds 38 distinct non-apparatus documents in 27 volumes dated 1893-08-18 to 1986-06-11 with no Ed2 volume, and docs/_retrieved.jsonl holds the 66 distinct pairs the memo counts. Lots 66D95 and 63D351 resolve to NAID 2839192 (matchType control) in central-files-index.json; 59D95 is a curated 'possible' match to Conference Files 602875 (A1 3051B), reported as probable. The bundle's index provenanceDigest, the shards manifest and the shard folder's .generation all read 89481b18…e6101 and documentOffset is 0.4.
